question: Do the January and February 2009 glass-eel samples reported by Yoshinaga et al. (2014) overlap with the broader monthly Cagayan estuary series reported by Aoyama et al. (2015)?

sources.citation: Yoshinaga, T., Aoyama, J., Shinoda, A., Watanabe, S., Azanza, R. V., & Tsukamoto, K. (2014). Occurrence and biological characteristics of glass eels of the Japanese eel Anguilla japonica at the Cagayan River of Luzon Island, Philippines in 2009. Zoological Studies, 53, 13. https://doi.org/10.1186/1810-522X-53-13
sources.reportedSampling: Glass eels were caught at the Cagayan River estuary in Aparri on 26 January and 19 February 2009 using an approximately 5 m set net. The paper reports n=309 and n=458 for those dates, 767 total; 52 January specimens classified as Anguilla japonica were genetically checked, while no A. japonica was identified in the February sample.
sources.identificationScope: The paper genetically checked all 52 specimens classified morphologically as A. japonica and a selected 32-specimen pigmented long-fin subsample. It reports no capture coordinates, sample identifiers, voucher/catalog IDs, or GenBank accessions for this catch.

sources.citation: Aoyama, J., Yoshinaga, T., Shinoda, A., Shirotori, F., Yambot, A. V., & Han, Y.-S. (2015). Seasonal Changes in Species Composition of Glass Eels of the Genus Anguilla (Teleostei: Anguillidae) Recruiting to the Cagayan River, Luzon Island, the Philippines. Pacific Science, 69(2), 263–270. https://doi.org/10.2984/69.2.8
sources.reportedSampling: Monthly set-net glass-eel samples at the Cagayan River mouth from May 2008 through September 2009 (Period I) and November 2011 through December 2012 (Period II). It reports 8,643 Period I specimens and 32,178 specimens overall. The paper describes a set net with a 5 m cod-end and 2 m wings on each side; monthly sample sizes varied and are not an absolute recruitment-abundance measure.
sources.relevantDiscussion: The discussion cites Yoshinaga et al. (2014) as reporting 52 A. japonica among 767 specimens sampled in 2009 from the same area, then says the present 32,178-specimen series found one A. japonica in February 2009. The figure caption also attributes one A. japonica to February 2009.

matchingSignals: Both studies sample glass eels at the Cagayan River mouth or estuary during dates in 2009.
The January and February 2009 dates fall inside Aoyama et al.'s broader May 2008-September 2009 Period I.
Both describe set-net collection of glass eels with approximately 5 m net dimensions.
Aoyama, Yoshinaga, and Shinoda are coauthors of both papers, and Aoyama et al. (2015) explicitly cites Yoshinaga et al. (2014)'s 52-of-767 result.
separationOrConflictSignals: Yoshinaga et al. (2014) report zero A. japonica in their 19 February 2009 sample; Aoyama et al. (2015) report one A. japonica in February 2009 in the broader series.

The 2014 paper provides two dated sample totals (309 and 458); the 2015 paper's accessible text gives an aggregate Period I total and monthly ranges but no retrievable sample identifier or explicit crosswalk to the 767 fish.

The papers describe identification workflows at different levels: Yoshinaga et al. genetically checked the 52 putative A. japonica and a selected long-fin subset, while Aoyama et al. describe broader Period I genetic identification and monthly subsampling details. Method differences do not by themselves establish whether physical specimens or catch events were shared.
lineageAssessment.conclusion: The papers are demonstrably related publication leads and may cover overlapping 2009 sampling, but the reviewed sources do not prove that Yoshinaga et al.'s 767 fish are a subset of, or independent from, Aoyama et al.'s monthly series. The conflicting February A. japonica report prevents a clean event-level reconciliation. Keep the relationship unresolved; do not describe the papers as either duplicate datasets or independent confirmations.
lineageAssessment.countingDecision: Keep 767 (2014) and 32,178 total / 8,643 Period I (2015) as separate source-reported study totals. Do not add them together, deduplicate them, scale the selected subsamples, or count either paper as independent confirmation of the other's species result until sample logs or an explicit author-provided crosswalk resolves lineage.

evidenceLimits: This evidence concerns glass-eel recruitment at one Cagayan estuary, not adult fish distribution across the Cagayan basin or its freshwater reaches, lakes, and tributaries.
The 2015 paper states that variable monthly sample totals do not represent absolute recruitment abundance.
No specimen identifiers, station/catch identifiers, capture-coordinate series, or voucher/accession crosswalk was found in the reviewed source texts.
The study locator maps are not capture-coordinate datasets and are not digitized as occurrence geometry.
Historical glass-eel recruitment does not establish present-day presence, resident adult range, catchability, diet, legal status, safety, or fishing-season advice.

The 2014 article states CC BY 2.0; no article-specific reuse license was identified for the 2015 article. No article tables, figures, or extended text are reproduced here, and no app projection is approved.
nextActions: Seek the original Aoyama et al. Table 1 page image or author-held monthly spreadsheet and compare the January and February 2009 monthly sample totals and taxon counts with Yoshinaga et al.'s dated samples.

If the table does not resolve the mismatch, request the sample/catch identifiers or field-log crosswalk from the corresponding author; keep all sample identities unresolved unless source evidence is supplied.
Continue Region II freshwater, brackish, estuary, lake, reservoir, wetland, and marine inventory work without promoting these estuary recruitment papers to a basin-wide checklist.
